sections.h2: Utah laws that cover landlords and tenants
sections.html:
Three parts of the Utah Code do most of the work: the Fit Premises Act (Utah Code Title 57, Chapter 22), the deposit rules in Chapter 17 of the same title, and the unlawful detainer provisions in Title 78B, Chapter 6, Part 8.

Between them they cover what a landlord must provide, what a tenant must do, how the deposit comes back and how a tenancy ends in court. If you plan to sell a rental, learn all three. A buyer's questions usually come straight out of them.

sections.h2: What a Utah landlord must provide
sections.html:
Under Utah Code 57-22-4 an owner may not rent a unit unless it is safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. The owner must also keep the systems listed in the statute in working order.

  • Common areas kept sanitary and safe.
  • Electrical, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water systems maintained.
  • Any air conditioning system kept working.
  • Appliances and facilities named in the rental agreement maintained.
  • In buildings with more than two units, garbage receptacles and removal, unless the parties agree otherwise.

At or before the start of the rental term the owner gives the renter, in writing, the owner's or agent's name, address and phone number, a signed copy of the rental agreement and any rules.

Before signing, the owner has to offer a condition inventory, a condition form or a walkthrough inspection.

Late fees cannot exceed the greater of 10% of the agreed rent or $75. An owner also can't charge a fee, fine or interest that is higher than the agreed amount or that is missing from the rental agreement.

The one exception is a month-to-month agreement, where a new charge needs 15 days written notice. Before taking an application fee, the owner must disclose a good faith estimate of rent and fixed non-rent expenses, the eligibility criteria and how the renter can get money back.

SituationLimit or deadline
Late feeGreater of 10% of rent or $75
New charge on a month-to-month tenancy15 days written notice
Landlord entry24 hours notice unless the agreement says otherwise
Prospective renter demands a refundWithin 5 business days after receiving the agreement
Owner pays the refundWithin 5 business days of the demand
Deposit return and itemization30 days after the renter vacates

Section 57-22-5 lists what the renter owes. The renter keeps the unit clean and safe, uses the plumbing, electrical and heating facilities reasonably and stays current on payments the rental agreement requires.

  • Follow local health board rules that affect health and safety.
  • Dispose of garbage in a clean and safe way.
  • Use the unit only for its designed purpose and respect the occupant limit.
  • Follow the rental agreement's rules, including smoking restrictions.

The same section bars a renter from damaging or removing parts of the unit, interfering with another renter's peaceful enjoyment, or unreasonably refusing the owner access for repairs. A tenant who isn't meeting these duties can't use the repair remedies described next.

sections.h2: What a tenant can do when repairs are needed
sections.html:
The tenant gives written notice that describes each problem, names the remedy chosen and allows the owner to enter. Utah Code 57-22-6 gives the owner three calendar days to fix a habitability problem and 10 calendar days to cure a violation of the rental agreement.

A condition that risks imminent loss of life or serious physical harm can be reported by any reasonable means. The owner must begin remedial action within 24 hours.

  • Rent abatement: if the owner doesn't take substantial action in time, rent is abated from the date of the notice and the agreement ends. The deposit and prorated prepaid rent are refunded, and the renter leaves within 10 days after the corrective period.
  • Repair and deduct: the renter makes the repair and subtracts the cost from future rent, up to two months' rent, and sends receipts to the owner within five calendar days after the next rental period starts.
  • Court: the renter may sue after the corrective period, and the summons requires the owner to appear within three business days.

An owner can also end the lease instead of repairing if the unit is unfit. That takes written notice by the end of the corrective period and refunds within 10 days. Either side can be ordered to pay costs and reasonable attorney fees.

Utah Code 57-17-3 lets the owner apply the deposit to unpaid rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, other contract costs and cleaning. The balance, any prepaid rent and an itemized written list of deductions are due within 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession.

If the owner is late, the renter can serve a Tenant's Notice to Provide Deposit Disposition, and the owner then has five business days to pay and itemize. After that the owner may owe the full deposit and prepaid rent plus a $100 penalty. A court that finds bad faith can add court costs and attorney fees.

Selling a rental raises the question of who holds the deposit afterward. Ask a Utah attorney or your title company how to handle the balance, and keep the ledger ready for the buyer.

The notice depends on the type of tenancy. The periods come from Utah Code 78B-6-802.

  • Unpaid rent: 3 business days to pay or surrender.
  • Violation of another lease covenant: 3 calendar days to perform or surrender.
  • Month-to-month: at least 15 calendar days before the end of the period.
  • Tenancy at will: at least 5 calendar days.
  • Fixed term that has expired: no notice required.

Notices are served under Utah Code 78B-6-805. That can mean handing the notice over, sending it by registered or certified mail, leaving a copy with a suitable person or posting it on the property. During the notice period the tenant may cure the violation and keep the lease.

A landlord who wins in court may be awarded rent plus three times the damages assessed in listed categories, along with costs and reasonable attorney fees, under Utah Code 78B-6-811.

sections.h2: Crime victims and calls for help
sections.html:
Utah Code 57-22-5.1 gives renters who are crime victims the right to have the lock changed if they provide a qualifying protective order or police report and pay for the work. The owner must refuse to give the new key to the alleged perpetrator.

A domestic violence victim who is current on lease obligations can end the lease by giving written notice, paying a termination fee equal to one month's rent and moving out within 15 days. An owner may not penalize or evict a renter for reasonable requests for help from police, fire, ambulance or medical services.

sections.h2: Selling a Utah rental with a tenant in place
sections.html:
Start with the paperwork, because a buyer or title company will ask for it. If the tenant is behind or the lease is ending, the notice periods above show how long a clean exit would take.

  • A copy of each signed lease and the required rental agreement disclosures.
  • The deposit amount, any prepaid rent and the ledger.
  • Written repair requests and any notice of deficient condition.
  • Any eviction notice served and where the case stands.
  • 24 hours notice for each showing, unless the rental agreement says otherwise.

Owners who inherited a rental, have a tenant who won't leave or have a unit that needs repairs they can't afford sometimes choose an as-is cash sale. Cash Home Buyers buys Utah houses in that condition and can walk you through what the closing would involve.

faqs.q: How much notice must a Utah landlord give before entering?
faqs.a: At least 24 hours, unless the rental agreement provides otherwise. Utah Code 57-22-4 sets this rule, and it also applies to showings when the owner is selling.

faqs.q: How long does a Utah landlord have to return a security deposit?
faqs.a: 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession. The landlord sends the balance, any prepaid rent and an itemized written list of deductions. If the deadline is missed, the renter can serve a notice and the landlord then has five business days to comply.

faqs.q: What is the maximum late fee in Utah?
faqs.a: The greater of 10% of the agreed rent or $75. A new charge not in the rental agreement is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy and needs 15 days written notice.

faqs.q: Can a Utah tenant withhold rent for repairs?
faqs.a: Not on their own. The tenant sends a written notice of deficient condition and waits out the corrective period, three calendar days for habitability and 10 for the rental agreement. If the owner still doesn't act, Utah Code 57-22-6 allows rent abatement or repair and deduct up to two months' rent.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Utah house that has a tenant in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners can sell a rented house, and some buyers purchase them as-is with the tenant still there. Gather the lease, deposit record and any notices first, and ask a Utah attorney how the sale affects the deposit and any pending case.
